chapter_theme: A song at Valikondapuram (வாலிகொண்டபுரம்): the poet scorns those who carry a carrion body yet swagger in wealth, with chowries, horns and palanquins, and asks that this desire burn and he be given love as a servant of the feet; the praise names Siva's dance and Murugan's own dance of victory.

898.reading: The poet describes those who carry a body that flies, ants, foxes, dogs, ghouls, vultures and crows will eat, yet call it fitting and speak arrogantly like a rutting elephant, boasting of their wealth, arms and minds, wearing cool garlands among dancing women, white chowries, horns and flutes, riding in palanquins to the end; he asks that the desire for that great life burn away, that desire for Murugan grow, and that, seeing the service of Siva, he be given love as a servant of the feet. The praise names Murugan who burned the Suras of the dark mountain of deceit, while Siva dances in the hall with Brahma, Indra and the gods worshipping, who danced in victory as the vidyadhara women rejoiced, and who came to guard the millet with Valli, at Valikondapuram.
898.nuance: The scavenger list opens the song, so the pomp that follows (வெண்கவரி, கொம்பு குழல், தண்டிகை) is seen as carried by a corpse to be. உனது பாத தொண்டனென அன்பு தாராய்: the plea asks for love as service. Two corrupt words in line 4 (§ர்¡லெ) leave a phrase unread.

links.note: Kural 37 says there is no need to state what virtue is: look at the palanquin's bearer and its rider (சிவிகை பொறுத்தானோடு ஊர்ந்தான் இடை), taking the rider's place as merit's fruit. 898 shows the rider in his palanquin (தண்டிகையில்) with chowries and horns, but opens with the body that flies, ants, foxes and crows will eat, and calls the pride arrogance like a rutting elephant's. Read together, the song limits the Kural's lesson: the rank may be the fruit of past virtue, but the one who rides is carrying a corpse to be.
